rationale: I followed the 11-09 performance playbook and the growth playbook's Lane A order. Injection site reactions and diarrhea both shipped as long-forms on 11-09. The next item, dehydration, was covered as a sick-day Short (11-04) and a carousel (11-06), so a long-form now would repeat that angle within 30 days. L1 is therefore burping and heartburn. It's evergreen, label-based and close to the big three, it answers a question no live video answers, and holiday meals make it timely. Its body rests on settled sources: label rates per dose vs placebo, the gastric-emptying mechanism and NHS/ACG reflux self-care. Both fresh news items go into Shorts, not long-form. S1 covers the FDA's class-wide NAION label change from 11-09, a caution topic. It gets a calm, label-first 'is this normal?' frame, and it corrects our own 11-09 Short, which said the tirzepatide label didn't list NAION. S2 is the 13:00 fresh-randomized-result slot: the Nature Medicine resistance-training RCT. It also gives the stalled Strength video a new hook. S3 is the 20:00 funnel Short and the required spin-off of L1, aimed at the Thanksgiving peak. The carousel reuses verified Short text only, because carousels reach 0–4 people. Mix: 2 rising/emerging news Shorts, 3 evergreen pieces, and S1 doubles as the calm myth correction. Body systems: eyes, muscle and GI (L1 and its spin-off), with the carousel on skin and injection sites. Pillars: get-the-most ×2, life-on-glp1 ×2, myths ×1.

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide burping and heartburn: how often the label reports belching, reflux and indigestion for each dose vs placebo, why slower stomach emptying can cause them, everyday habits that may help, and the signs that mean seeing a clinician
pieces.angle: Keep the angle as written, with these exact fixes: chapter 4 says 'NHS advises not eating within 3 or 4 hours before bed, and raising the head of the bed by around 10 to 20 cm instead of adding pillows'. The NHS trigger list is quoted exactly and framed as 'may trigger it for some people'. Chapter 6 credits to NHS only the triggers its pages actually print. Vomiting blood, black stools and chest pain are untagged urgent signs → 'your local urgent care or emergency number'. 'Sulfur burps' is called a commonly described symptom, with no explanation of the cause.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide Burping and Heartburn: What Helps
pieces.why: It's the next unanswered Lane A side-effect question next to the big three. The label rates and NHS guidance can be verified in depth, and holiday meals make it timely. | fact-check: This is a good Lane A topic. Burping (eructation), dyspepsia and GERD are all listed among the Zepbound label's most common adverse reactions (≥5%), so the per-dose vs placebo rates exist. Copy them exactly from the 28 Aug 2026 label table (pi.lilly.com/us/zepbound-uspi.pdf), keep the pooled-trial population, and don't pool the arms. Three corrections to the angle: (a) The NHS heartburn page (nhs.uk/conditions/heartburn-and-acid-reflux, last reviewed 20 Nov 2023, next review due 20 Nov 2026, so re-check the live date before citing) says 'do not eat within 3 or 4 hours before bed'. It does NOT say 'avoid lying down for 3 hours after eating'. Use the NHS wording or drop the tag. For raising the head of the bed, NHS says 'by around 10 to 20cm, so your chest and head are above your waist' and not to use extra pillows. Credit the trigger foods only as NHS lists them ('coffee, tomatoes, alcohol, chocolate and fatty or spicy foods'), and say these are things that may trigger it for some people, never 'bad' foods. (b) The NHS see-a-GP triggers are heartburn most days, pharmacy medicines not helping, food getting stuck, being sick often, and losing weight for no reason. 'Vomiting blood' and 'black stools' must be found on the NHS indigestion page before they're credited to NHS; otherwise present them as untagged warning signs that need same-day care. Don't use NHS 111 alone; use 'your local urgent care or emergency number'. (c) No source supports anything specific about 'sulfur burps', so call it a commonly described symptom and attach no mechanism. Delayed gastric emptying should be described in label wording, and 'food sitting longer' is a likely explanation, not a proven cause. All the other guardrails in the angle are correct and should stay: the pancreatitis and gallbladder label wording, chest pain → emergency number, the scoped don't-stop line, the hypoglycemia caveat for people on insulin or a sulfonylurea, the pharmacist line with no products, and the prescriber line.

pieces.topic: FDA's class-wide label change (Nov 9, 2026) adding NAION, a rare sudden vision loss, to warnings and precautions for all GLP-1 medicines including tirzepatide, and how it differs from temporary blurry vision
pieces.angle: Title: 'Tirzepatide and Vision: What the FDA Just Added #shorts', or 'Will Tirzepatide Affect Your Eyes? #shorts'. Open: 'The FDA has added a rare eye condition called NAION to the warnings for all GLP-1 medicines, including tirzepatide. Here's what that means and the signs to know.' Give the absolute rate: about 6 vs 4 cases per 100,000 person-years in pooled trials, GLP-1 medicines vs comparison medicines. Say the FDA notes cases have been reported with every marketed GLP-1. Contrast this without dismissing blurry vision: blurry vision can also happen when blood sugar changes quickly, so any new or changing vision is worth telling your clinician about. Then the FDA signs: sudden painless vision loss in one eye, which you may notice on waking; blind spots or tunnel vision; colours looking off; blurry or hazy spots. Any of these → contact your healthcare professional right away, or your local urgent care or emergency number. Then the scoped don't-stop line, regular eye exams (especially with diabetes), the Exp F line, 'Not personal advice', the prescriber line and the closing line. Source: the FDA DSC only. Use no eye-damage imagery and no smiling or check-mark mascot.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide Blurry Vision: Is This Normal? #shorts
pieces.why: The radar rates it the top-momentum (95) caution story. Coverage is driven by scary headlines, so a calm, label-first take fills a gap and fits our best Short format. It also updates our 11-09 eye Short, which said the label didn't list NAION. | fact-check: Verified: on 9 Nov 2026 the FDA issued a Drug Safety Communication requiring all GLP-1 RA labels to add NAION to Warnings and Precautions (fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-communications/fda-requires-safety-labeling-changes-glucagon-peptide-1-receptor-agonists-glp-1-ras-due-potential). Zepbound and Mounjaro are named. Problems in the angle: (1) The FDA does NOT say semaglutide is 'studied most'. It says 'NAION cases have been reported for all currently marketed GLP-1 RA products', and its estimate pooled 126 RCTs across multiple GLP-1 RAs: 6.4 vs 3.8 cases per 100,000 person-years (GLP-1 RA vs placebo or non-GLP-1 glucose-lowering medicine). Use that absolute-rate framing instead. (2) 'Most common in adults 50 and over' isn't an FDA claim about risk on GLP-1s. The FDA only gives the background incidence in adults over 50. Drop it, or state it exactly as background incidence. (3) The FDA lists 'blurred or missing portions of vision' and 'reduced central sharpness (e.g., blurry or hazy spots)' as NAION symptoms. So the hook 'Usually it's not what the headlines describe' and the 'Is this normal?' title play down a symptom the FDA says needs prompt action. That's the main safety problem. (4) The FDA's patient action is 'contact their health care professional right away'. Use that wording, and you can add 'or your local urgent care or emergency number' for sudden vision loss. Symptoms: 'sudden, painless vision loss in one eye that patients may notice upon waking' ('may', not 'often'), blind spots or tunnel vision, distortion of colours, blurry or hazy spots. (5) The FDA says people who have had NAION should talk with their health care professional about whether to continue. Keep the scoped don't-stop line. Calling this 'one new fact' is fine for a 13:00-style news fact, but it's in the 08:00 slot, so the title needs the calm 'Will it…?' form without false reassurance.

pieces.topic: First RCT of supervised resistance training plus tirzepatide (Nature Medicine, Nov 9, 2026): 120 adults (60 men, 60 postmenopausal women), 61 on tirzepatide alone vs 59 on tirzepatide plus training
pieces.angle: Answer within 10 s: 'In a randomized trial of adults aged 50 to 70 on tirzepatide, the group who did resistance training 3 times a week got stronger, while the tirzepatide-only group got weaker.' Every number comes from the Nature Medicine paper or its PubMed record: the strength measure, % change per arm, lean-mass kg per arm, and the 40-week timeframe. Name both arms (61 vs 59), say it was one small, single-centre trial without type 2 diabetes, and say the trainers lost less lean mass, not none. Takeaway: WHO recommends muscle-strengthening on at least 2 days a week; start gently and check with your clinician if you have health conditions. Include a protein food at meals unless your clinician limits protein. Add one GI line, the Exp F line, 'Not personal advice', the prescriber line and the closing line. Title: 'Tirzepatide Muscle Loss: Does Lifting Help? #shorts'.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide Muscle Loss: Does Lifting Actually Help? #shorts
pieces.why: It's a fresh randomized result published Nov 9 that few creators have yet. It sits right next to the stalled Strength video and can feed that video a new hook. | fact-check: Verified: the T-REx trial was published in Nature Medicine in November 2026 (nature.com/articles/s41591-026-04752-5; UWA dates it 10 Nov, so say 'November 2026', not 'Nov 9'). It was single-centre: 120 adults aged 50–70 with overweight or obesity and no type 2 diabetes (60 men, 60 postmenopausal women), randomized to tirzepatide alone (n=61) or tirzepatide plus resistance training (n=59), with three 1-hour sessions a week for 40 weeks. It was investigator-initiated, and the manufacturer supplied the drug. The UWA release says strength rose about 10% with training and fell about 10% without it, and that trainers lost 25% less lean tissue. That's a relative figure, so give the absolute kg from the paper as well. The paper redirects to a login page, so the scriptwriter must take the exact figures from the paper or its PubMed record and must not use the UWA numbers. Fixes: (1) 'First randomized trial' is the university's claim, and other RCTs (FLEX, RESIST-26) are under way. Say 'one of the first randomized trials' unless the paper itself says 'first'. (2) Only say 'supervised' if the paper says so. (3) Name the population (aged 50–70, no type 2 diabetes) and the dose of training actually tested (3 sessions a week for 40 weeks), and make clear that WHO's 'at least 2 days a week' is general guidance, not what the trial tested. (4) Lean mass isn't the same as strength; keep that line. (5) A body-worry Short is fine, but don't promise to prevent muscle loss; the trial showed less lean loss, not none. (6) Add a caveat: check with your clinician before starting a new exercise programme if you have heart, joint or other health conditions.

It might, because tirzepatide can slow how fast food leaves your stomach (label wording), and a full stomach can push acid upward.' New fact: one label heartburn/GERD rate per dose arm vs placebo, matching L1's verified script exactly. Our own untagged tips: a smaller first plate, eating slowly, stopping when comfortably full. 'Stay upright after eating' is credited to NHS only if NHS says it. Ask a pharmacist before any antacid. Red flags as in L1, including chest pain → local emergency number. No guilt, no foods labelled 'bad', and no date words. 'Don't stop or change your medicines on your own', 'Not personal advice', the prescriber line, then the closing line. No Exp F line and no spoken titles. Related-video target: L1 once it's verified live, otherwise the Thanksgiving long-form. Log the target in the post notes.
